title: An Entire Town Lives in One Building. Blame the Army.
question: Why do people live in Whittier?
message: This video tells curious adults that almost a whole Alaskan town lives in one building because the US Army built a hidden wartime port there, and in that weather, one building is the sensible choice.
angle: People live in Whittier because the US Army picked this foggy, ice-free inlet for a wartime port, drilled a tunnel to reach it and left behind a fourteen-storey building that became the town, despite a one-lane tunnel with a bedtime, around five metres of rain and snow a year and a winter with almost no one around.

And by the end of this trip, I had to decide whether I could live there too.

scenes.narration: Whittier is about fifty-eight miles from Anchorage. That's roughly ninety-three kilometres. Easy drive, I thought. I had snacks, a full tank, and the timetable folded in the glovebox, unread. That detail will matter. The road runs along the water, past glaciers hanging off the mountains, and then it runs straight into a mountain. There is one way in by car, and it is a tunnel. I pulled into the waiting area with a sandwich and a theory. My theory was bears. Surely a tunnel that closes at night is keeping out bears. I ate the sandwich and watched for bears. The bears did not come. A train did.

scenes.narration: The real reason is less furry. The tunnel is two and a half miles long, about four kilometres, and it has one lane. Cars and trains share it, so they take turns. In winter it opens one direction, then the other, about every half hour. And it goes to bed. In winter the gates lock at eleven at night and open again at seven. The last run into town leaves at ten thirty. I arrived just after it left. The Alaska Railroad calls this the longest combined rail and highway tunnel in North America. From the outside, at night, it is mostly a very long closed door. I slept in the car. My breath froze on the window in the shape of the word NOPE.

scenes.narration: Next morning I drove through. On the far side: a deep grey inlet, waterfalls, mountains straight up from the sea. I made a guess. People came here for the view. Then the clouds came down and the view left. That guess did not survive breakfast. Long before any soldiers, this pass was part of a portage route used by the Chugach people of Prince William Sound. It was a way to carry boats and goods between the waters. But a route is not a town. So why build a town at the end of a tunnel at the end of a road? I went to the little town museum. Short answer: the Second World War.

scenes.narration: Here is what I learned, and it surprised me. The bad weather was the point. During the war, the US Army wanted a supply port for Alaska. Whittier gave them a shorter trip than the port at Seward, about fifty-two miles shorter by sea. Ships spent less time exposed to submarines. The water in the inlet does not freeze. And according to the Alaska Department of Transportation, the Army picked the spot because the cloud and fog would hide the port from Japanese bombers. Picture hiding under a blanket that never gets washed, and the blanket is the size of the sky. Then they drilled through the mountain for a railway, finished in nineteen forty-three. By the mid nineteen forties, more than a thousand soldiers and workers were here. My bear theory was officially retired.

scenes.narration: After the war, the Army built big. The building everyone lives in now was finished in the late nineteen fifties, as housing for soldiers and their families. It is actually three blocks joined into one. The Army left in nineteen sixty. In nineteen seventy-two the city bought the buildings, and people moved in. So I spent a day inside it. I set an alarm, put on my socks, and did not put on shoes. Eight in the morning: post office, ground floor, near the entrance. Nine: the police station, down the same hall. I did not need the police. I just wanted to say I had walked to it in my socks. The hallway did not look surprised. I suspect it has seen plenty of socks.

scenes.narration: Mid-morning: the clinic. Late morning: the church. Lunchtime: laundry, a couple of floors down, in the elevator, holding a basket like a man with nowhere to be. There are two small shops, the city offices and a playground. The school is across the street, and the children get there through a tunnel underground. Another tunnel. This town really likes tunnels. By mid-afternoon I had done every errand of a normal week and never seen the sky. My coat was still dry on its hook. And here is the strange part. I liked it. Quiet halls, warm rooms, neighbours who nod at you in the elevator. I changed my mind. Maybe I could live here.

scenes.narration: Then I stepped outside. One snowflake landed on my nose. Then its family arrived. Then its neighbours. Then, as far as I could tell, everyone it had ever met. According to the state's weather records, Whittier gets around one hundred and ninety-six inches of rain and snow a year combined. That's about five metres. The snow alone averages around twenty feet. Reporters who spent a winter here describe winds of about sixty miles an hour. I opened my umbrella. The umbrella left for Anchorage without me. I assume it caught the tunnel in time.

scenes.narration: Back inside, dripping, I finally got it. In a place like this, one building is not weird. It is the sensible answer. Picture keeping your whole life inside one fridge on purpose, because outside the fridge is worse. No shovelling a path between home and school. No walk to the post office in sideways snow. No scraping ice off the car just to buy milk. In winter, the town gets very quiet. Many businesses here even disconnect their phones from October to April. The tourists are gone, the boats are out of the water, and the building hums along like a ship at anchor. So I changed my mind again. Living in the building, yes. Living in this winter, no thank you.

scenes.narration: Across from the tower stands a second building, and nobody lives in it. The Buckner Building was finished in nineteen fifty-three. It was called the city under one roof, before the tower took that job. It was used for only a few years, then abandoned. Today it is broken windows and concrete, still standing because it is very hard to knock down. I stood outside it for a long time.

scenes.narration: There is a harder story here too, and I want to tell it plainly. On March the twenty-seventh, nineteen sixty-four, a huge earthquake shook southern Alaska. In Whittier, the shaking and the waves that followed killed thirteen people. At the time, only about seventy people were living here. The waterfront was wrecked. The town rebuilt, slowly. When people here talk about weather and mountains, they are not complaining. They are paying attention.

scenes.narration: I went back in July. Same tunnel, same timetable, very different town. The snow was gone. The mountains were green, and every one of them seemed to have a waterfall. In summer the tunnel opens earlier and closes later, and I made it through with time to spare. The harbour was full of boats. The port the Army built is still in use. Big cruise ships start and end their trips here. Tour boats leave the small boat harbour for the fjords, where you can see more than two dozen glaciers in a single day. I started counting glaciers, then a sea otter floated past on its back, and I lost count.

scenes.narration: That is the other half of the answer. Summer is when this town works. Fishing charters go out for halibut and salmon. People rent kayaks and paddle up to the ice. The same deep, ice-free water that made the Army happy now makes visitors happy. Plenty of the people who run those boats in summer go home at night to the same tall building. And the people who stay through winter keep the lights on in it, together. I asked myself the big question on the water, holding a fishing rod I did not know how to use. The fish knew. The fish was not interested.

scenes.chapter: Would I Take the Elevator Home?
scenes.role: về bàn: ghép các mảnh 'vì sao', phán quyết SUMMER ONLY, callback tờ lịch giờ, câu hỏi kéo bình luận
scenes.narration: So here is how it fits together. A war needed a hidden port. The fog hid it. A tunnel reached it. The Army left a building, and the weather made that building the town. Nobody chose one building to be strange. They chose it because walking to school through a tunnel beats wading through a winter of snow. Would I move there? In July, I would carry my own bags through that tunnel. In February, I would be the person sleeping in the car outside it. My verdict is SUMMER ONLY. It suits people who love boats, quiet and knowing all their neighbours by floor number. It does not suit anyone who hates elevators or deadlines. I pinned the timetable to my wall. I check it before I go to bed now. Could you spend a whole winter without leaving one building?

claims.quote: outside a town where most people share one front door
claims.statement: Most residents of Whittier, Alaska live in a single building, Begich Towers.

claims.quote: At the last census it had two hundred and seventy-two people.
claims.statement: Whittier, Alaska had a population of 272 at the 2020 United States census.

claims.quote: Most of them live in one fourteen-storey building.
claims.statement: Most residents of Whittier, Alaska live in a single 14-storey building, Begich Towers.

claims.quote: Whittier is about fifty-eight miles from Anchorage. That's roughly ninety-three kilometres.
claims.statement: Whittier, Alaska is about 58 miles (about 93 km) from Anchorage.

claims.quote: There is one way in by car, and it is a tunnel.
claims.statement: The only road access to Whittier, Alaska is through the Anton Anderson Memorial Tunnel.

claims.quote: The tunnel is two and a half miles long, about four kilometres, and it has one lane. Cars and trains share it, so they take turns.
claims.statement: The only road access to Whittier, Alaska is the Anton Anderson Memorial Tunnel, a 2.5-mile (about 4 km) single-lane tunnel shared by cars and trains, which alternate.

claims.quote: In winter it opens one direction, then the other, about every half hour.
claims.statement: In the winter schedule, the Whittier tunnel alternates direction, with each direction opening roughly every 30 minutes.

claims.quote: In winter the gates lock at eleven at night and open again at seven. The last run into town leaves at ten thirty.
claims.statement: In the winter schedule (October 1 to April 30), the Whittier tunnel gates lock at 11:00 pm and the tunnel reopens at 7:00 am; the last opening into Whittier is at 10:30 pm.

claims.quote: The Alaska Railroad calls this the longest combined rail and highway tunnel in North America.
claims.statement: According to the Alaska Railroad, the Anton Anderson Memorial Tunnel is the longest combined rail-and-highway tunnel in North America.

claims.quote: Long before any soldiers, this pass was part of a portage route used by the Chugach people of Prince William Sound.
claims.statement: Before the military town was built, the area of Whittier was part of a portage route used by the Chugach people native to Prince William Sound.

claims.quote: During the war, the US Army wanted a supply port for Alaska. Whittier gave them a shorter trip than the port at Seward, about fifty-two miles shorter by sea. Ships spent less time exposed to submarines.
claims.statement: During World War II the US Army chose Whittier as a supply port partly because the voyage was shorter than to Seward (a trip to Seward added about 52 miles) and reduced ships' exposure to Japanese submarines.

claims.quote: The water in the inlet does not freeze.
claims.statement: The waters of Passage Canal at Whittier, Alaska remain ice-free year-round.

claims.quote: according to the Alaska Department of Transportation, the Army picked the spot because the cloud and fog would hide the port from Japanese bombers
claims.statement: According to the Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities, the US military selected Whittier's location because cloud and fog cover would protect the port from Japanese bombing during World War II.

claims.quote: Then they drilled through the mountain for a railway, finished in nineteen forty-three. By the mid nineteen forties, more than a thousand soldiers and workers were here.
claims.statement: The US Army built a railway spur with tunnels to Whittier, completed in 1943, and by the mid-1940s Whittier's population of military and civilian personnel exceeded 1,000.

claims.quote: The building everyone lives in now was finished in the late nineteen fifties, as housing for soldiers and their families. It is actually three blocks joined into one.
claims.statement: Begich Towers in Whittier (formerly the Hodge Building) was built for Army personnel and families and completed in 1957, combining east, middle and west sections built between 1953 and 1957.

claims.quote: The Army left in nineteen sixty. In nineteen seventy-two the city bought the buildings, and people moved in.
claims.statement: The US Army maintained Whittier until 1960, and in 1972 the City of Whittier purchased the Cold War-era buildings that now house most residents.

claims.quote: Eight in the morning: post office, ground floor, near the entrance. Nine: the police station, down the same hall.
claims.statement: Begich Towers contains Whittier's post office, near the entrance, and the police station down the same hallway.

claims.quote: There are two small shops, the city offices and a playground. The school is across the street, and the children get there through a tunnel underground.
claims.statement: Begich Towers contains a clinic, a church, a laundromat, two convenience stores, city offices and a playground, and Whittier's school across the street is reached through an underground tunnel.

claims.quote: According to the state's weather records, Whittier gets around one hundred and ninety-six inches of rain and snow a year combined. That's about five metres. The snow alone averages around twenty feet.
claims.statement: According to Alaska DOT&PF climate data (1942–2011), Whittier's average annual precipitation is about 196 inches (about 5 m), and average annual snowfall is about 20 feet.

claims.quote: Reporters who spent a winter here describe winds of about sixty miles an hour.
claims.statement: Journalists reporting on Whittier describe winter winds of around 60 miles per hour.

claims.quote: Many businesses here even disconnect their phones from October to April.
claims.statement: Many businesses in Whittier, Alaska disconnect their phones from October through April.

claims.quote: The Buckner Building was finished in nineteen fifty-three. It was called the city under one roof, before the tower took that job. It was used for only a few years, then abandoned.
claims.statement: The Buckner Building in Whittier, completed in 1953 and once called the 'city under one roof', was used for only a few years before being abandoned.

claims.quote: On March the twenty-seventh, nineteen sixty-four, a huge earthquake shook southern Alaska. In Whittier, the shaking and the waves that followed killed thirteen people. At the time, only about seventy people were living here.
claims.statement: The Alaska earthquake of March 27, 1964 killed 13 people in Whittier, which at the time had about 70 residents, and wrecked its waterfront.

claims.quote: In summer the tunnel opens earlier and closes later
claims.statement: The Whittier tunnel's summer schedule (May 1 to September 30) runs from 5:30 am to 11:15 pm, longer than the winter schedule of 7:00 am to 10:45 pm.

claims.quote: The port the Army built is still in use. Big cruise ships start and end their trips here.
claims.statement: The Port of Whittier, built by the US Army, is still in use, and cruise ships start or end voyages there.

claims.quote: Tour boats leave the small boat harbour for the fjords, where you can see more than two dozen glaciers in a single day.
claims.statement: Day tours from Whittier's small boat harbour into Prince William Sound can show visitors more than two dozen glaciers in one day.

claims.quote: Fishing charters go out for halibut and salmon. People rent kayaks and paddle up to the ice.
claims.statement: Fishing charters from Whittier target halibut and salmon, and visitors can rent kayaks to paddle in Prince William Sound near glaciers.

claims.quote: A war needed a hidden port. The fog hid it. A tunnel reached it. The Army left a building
claims.statement: Whittier was founded as a World War II Army port chosen partly for cloud cover, connected by a railway tunnel, and the Army left behind the building where most residents now live.
